Lessons.Title: Representing Exponential Decay
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: represent exponential decrease by y=a·b^t with 0<b<1 using equations, tables and graphs; interpret the initial amount and decay factor; distinguish measured discrete samples from continuous-time interpolation. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 5, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/5/preparation.html and student tasks https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/5/index.html (CC BY 4.0). Source includes an algae area model and insulin context; our first-party model is not a biological dose or medical instruction.

Original hypothetical surface staining area in square centimetres decreases by half after each treatment week. Initial area256cm², so A(t)=256(1/2)^t for nonnegative whole weeks t, giving 256,128,64,32,16 at weeks0–4. The formula can be evaluated at fractional weeks as a mathematical extension, but no physical process at fractional times is established without observations.

Read the graph: vertical intercept (0,256), positive y-values decreasing toward0 but never exactly0 at finite nonnegative t under the real exponential model. For t3 A=32; solving A=16 by pattern gives t4. An automatic assumption that all exponential decay crosses the horizontal axis at a finite time is incorrect.

Student task: use a table and original graph to identify multiplier, initial value and long-term trend; explain why discrete observed weeks may not prove smooth decay, and compare it with a linear decline. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for arithmetic, equation/graph match, context and asymptote interpretation, and disclosure of continuous-model assumptions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decay equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: An exponential decrease uses initial a>0 and a factor between0 and1.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read a from t0 and b from equal-step ratios.

KeyConcepts.Title: Long-term behavior
KeyConcepts.Definition: For 0<b<1 and a>0, outputs approach zero without reaching it at any finite real t.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not infer a zero from rounding small values.

KeyConcepts.Title: Discrete versus continuous
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rule can be extended to fractional inputs, but measurements may exist only at integer times.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State the model input domain separately.
KeyConcepts.Example: Weekly sampled spots only verify integer-week data.

WorkedExamples.Title: Complete decay table
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate A(t)=256×(1/2)^t for weeks0–4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret multiplier and initial value
WorkedExamples.Question: What do256 and1/2 represent?
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
Steps: Each equal week retains half the previous area.
This is50% reduction each week, not a50cm² reduction.
WorkedExamples.Check: Remainder ratio matches each table step.

WorkedExamples.Title: Understand graph asymptote
WorkedExamples.Question: Does A(t)=256(1/2)^t equal zero at a finite t?
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
Steps: For every finite real t, (1/2)^t is positive.
As t increases without bound, the factor tends toward zero.
The horizontal axis is approached but never crossed in the mathematical model.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No finite zero; horizontal asymptote A=0.
WorkedExamples.Check: At t4 the area is still16, not zero.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Concluding halving eventually produces exact zero in finitely many steps
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Powers of positive1/2 never equal zero.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate practical detection limits from mathematical limit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating discrete observations as proof of continuous-time kinetics
Using a medical example to imply dosing decisions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Mathematical decay alone is insufficient for clinical decisions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the example fictional and nonmedical.

SummaryPoints: The original invented surface-area values halve each week.
Exponential output remains positive, approaching zero asymptotically.
Context, sampling and graph choices require teacher review.
